import struct
C1=0xf4243
add=0x11
mul=0xeeeeeeeeeeeeeeef
add2=0x4444444444444444
cmp=0x1111111111111110
vals=[]
for l in range(0,200):
    rdx=(l*C1 + add) & ((1<<64)-1)
    rdx=(rdx*rdx) & ((1<<64)-1)
    rdx=(rdx+2) & ((1<<64)-1)
    rdx=(rdx*mul) & ((1<<64)-1)
    rdx=(rdx+add2) & ((1<<64)-1)
    if rdx<=cmp:
        vals.append((l,rdx))
print('count',len(vals))
print(vals[:20])
print('max l',max([l for l,_ in vals], default=None))

add=0x11
mul=0xeeeeeeeeeeeeeeef

cmp=0x1111111111111110
mask=(1<<64)-1

    rdx=(rdx*mul) & mask

import sys

with open(path,'rb') as f:

    ro=elf.get_section_by_name('.rodata')
    data=ro.data()
    vaddr=ro['sh_addr']
    def get(addr, n):
        off=addr - vaddr
        return data[off:off+n]
    for a in [0x402004,0x402016,0x40201f,0x402040]:
        b=get(a,64)
        s=b.split(b'\x00')[0]
        print(hex(a), 'bytes', b[:32].hex())
        print('string', s)
    # print whole table at 0x402040 up to 0x402040+0x19
    tab=get(0x402040,0x19)
    print('table',tab,tab.hex())

retrieved_cards.title: XOR-then-compare: recover the input by XORing the target back
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A byte-wise XOR with a constant (single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent key) is applied to the input before it is compared against a constant byte sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: XOR is its own inverse; the compared bytes are input XOR key, so the visible target is the encoded form, not the input.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Read the key and whether it is single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent; XOR the target back; then XOR the recovered input forward again and check it reproduces the compared bytes exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The XORed/compared bytes are the flag, or the check is 'encrypted' and not worth pursuing.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: XOR the comparison target back with the same key to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no XOR appears on the comparison path
the XOR is applied to an unrelated buffer, not the input being checked
misfire_risks: the key may be position-dependent / rolling rather than a single constant byte; assuming a single-byte key yields a wrong pre-image -- verify the key schedule before inverting
minimum_evidence_before_use: an XOR operation is observed between the input and the comparison
the XOR operand (key) is identifiable or recoverable

retrieved_cards.title: Compared against a one-way digest: do NOT try to invert it
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: The input is compared against a fixed-length, high-entropy constant produced by a one-way function (hash/checksum); the transform is not reversible.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: Unlike invertible encodings, a digest cannot be reversed to the input; the visible digest is the comparison target, submitting it raw fails, and inverting it is also futile.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Identify the function as one-way; redirect effort to finding or constraining the pre-image rather than inverting; confirm a candidate by computing the digest of the candidate yourself and checking it equals the compared constant.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Submit the digest, or attempt to 'decrypt'/invert the hash to recover the input.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Recognize a one-way function: the accepted input must be found another way (located in the binary/inputs, or recovered by a constrained search), not by inverting the digest.
not_applicable_when: the transform is actually reversible (XOR/shift/encoding -- use the matching card and invert)
the constant is not a digest of the input
misfire_risks: mislabeling a reversible transform as one-way stops a valid inversion; distinguish a true digest (fixed length, avalanche) from an invertible encoding before abandoning inversion
minimum_evidence_before_use: the comparison target is a fixed-length high-entropy constant
the producing function matches a known one-way construction

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract one-way-digest counter-case; no task-specific hashes or constants.

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

retrieval_event.query: Disassembly shows main takes argv[1], computes strlen, then if length==0x19 (25) it checks each byte i: expected_table[i] == ((input[i] XOR (edx&0xff))&0xff) where edx starts 0x62 and is updated edx += input[i]. The expected_table is 25 bytes at .rodata 0x402040. Therefore input can be reconstructed by iterating i=0..24: input[i] = expected_table[i] XOR (edx&0xff), then edx += input[i]. Applying this inversion to the table yields ASCII string FLAG{quartz_granite_6483} (length 25), which should satisfy the checker loop and print Correct.
